Family Health

The contraceptive implant: how it works and what to consider

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A contraceptive implant can suit someone who wants reliable pregnancy prevention without remembering a daily pill. Choosing it still involves personal preferences, a medical review and a plan for changes in bleeding. Understanding the particular product and your local instructions matters more than assuming that every implant has the same replacement date.

What the implant is and how it works

An implant is a small flexible rod placed just under the skin of the upper arm by a trained clinician. The commonly used etonogestrel implant is about 4 cm long. It releases a progestin, a manufactured hormone with progesterone-like effects, rather than estrogen.

It mainly prevents ovulation and thickens cervical mucus, making it harder for sperm to reach an egg. It also changes the uterine lining. Describing it only as preventing implantation misses its main action; it is contraception, not a treatment to end an established pregnancy.

How long it lasts: check the product and country

Older information often gives three years. In January 2026, the United States FDA approved Nexplanon for up to five years, with removal by the end of year five. Current NHS information also describes five-year use.

Do not apply that duration automatically to every brand or country. Ask the service to confirm your product, insertion date and current locally recommended replacement date. If your card says three years, ask whether updated guidance applies to you rather than extending use on your own.

Effectiveness and protection from infections

The implant is over 99% effective: fewer than one in 100 users become pregnant during a year of use. It does not depend on taking a pill correctly each day, but correct placement, replacement timing and interacting medicines still matter. No method makes pregnancy impossible.

It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. Correct and consistent condom use reduces infection risk; vaccination, testing and HIV prevention care may also be relevant. A condom is not an absolute guarantee against every infection.

Benefits, breastfeeding and return of fertility

Long-lasting protection, no daily task and no interruption during sex are practical advantages. An estrogen-free method may suit some people who cannot use estrogen, although that does not make it appropriate for everyone.

The implant can be used while breastfeeding under clinical guidance. The recommended timing after birth and need for extra protection depend on local guidance and circumstances; national practice guidance and product labeling can differ. Tell the service when you gave birth and how you feed your baby.

Some users have lighter bleeding or less period pain, but others do not. Reduced blood loss may help someone who bleeds less; the implant is not a guaranteed treatment for anemia. Fertility can return quickly after removal, without guaranteeing an immediate pregnancy.

Bleeding changes are common and can persist

Periods may become lighter, absent, irregular, more frequent or prolonged. Spotting is common and heavy bleeding is uncommon. Older etonogestrel trial data describe no bleeding in about one in five users; individual patterns vary.

Changes may improve, persist or change again; improvement after a few months is not guaranteed. Absent periods on the implant usually do not require treatment, but a sudden change or pregnancy symptoms may warrant a test and advice.

Discuss troublesome bleeding with the service. They may check for pregnancy, infection, medicine interactions or another cause, and offer treatment or removal according to your preferences. You do not have to tolerate unacceptable bleeding until the replacement date.

Who needs a careful suitability review

Tell the clinician about possible pregnancy, unexplained vaginal bleeding, breast cancer or another hormone-sensitive cancer, active liver disease or liver tumors, blood clots, stroke or heart disease, and allergy to implant components. These can affect whether the product is suitable; the current US Nexplanon label lists several as contraindications.

Also mention depression, diabetes, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol or triglycerides, gallbladder disease, seizures and allergies to local anesthetic or antiseptic. These are not all automatic exclusions, but may change monitoring, product choice or the medicine-interaction review.

A BMI of 30 or above does not by itself mean an implant will fail or that you cannot use one. CDC guidance permits implant use with obesity. Discuss your individual health and the actual product rather than treating body size as an effectiveness cutoff.

Other symptoms and procedure-related risks

Headache, breast tenderness, acne, weight change, dizziness, nausea, abdominal or back pain and mood changes have been reported. Reports do not prove that the implant caused every symptom. Changes in sexual desire or vaginal dryness deserve discussion rather than an automatic attribution to the implant.

Glucose and lipid changes may matter particularly for people with diabetes or related risks; monitoring can be appropriate. Enlarged ovarian follicles or cysts can occur and often resolve themselves, but new or severe pelvic pain needs assessment. Do not assume a painful abdomen is only a harmless cyst.

Fitting and removal can cause bruising, pain, scarring or infection. Deep placement, nerve or blood-vessel injury and migration are uncommon but important risks. A trained professional should fit, locate and remove the implant; never cut it out or attempt a home procedure.

Starting or switching without a protection gap

The clinician first assesses whether pregnancy can reasonably be excluded. An implant can often be fitted at another point in the cycle; it is not restricted to the first five days. Under CDC guidance, insertion within those first five days needs no extra protection; later insertion usually needs condoms or avoiding pregnancy-risk intercourse for seven days.

Do not stop hormonal contraception for a week before fitting as a general rule. Switching may require continuing the previous method briefly or coordinating removal of an IUD. Ask for exact instructions based on your current method, recent sex, birth or pregnancy loss.

If there has been a gap, possible pregnancy or sex without adequate protection, tell the service promptly. Emergency contraception and follow-up testing may be needed; the choice and timing require advice because hormonal methods can interact with some emergency pills.

Fitting and looking after the arm

Fitting normally uses local anesthetic and takes only a short appointment. You and the clinician should be able to feel the rod afterward. Get the product details, date, replacement plan and advice on checking it without repeatedly pressing the area.

Follow the service’s wound instructions. For Nexplanon, the US patient information describes keeping the pressure bandage for 24 hours and the smaller dressing clean and dry for three to five days. Your clinician may give instructions suited to the actual procedure.

If the implant cannot be felt, seems to have moved, becomes exposed, or the arm develops increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge, numbness or weakness, contact the service promptly. Use additional pregnancy protection until its presence and effectiveness are confirmed if it cannot be located. Do not probe for it yourself.

Medicines can change the protection

Give the prescriber a complete list of medicines and herbal products. Some enzyme-inducing medicines, including certain seizure medicines, rifampicin-type antibiotics and some HIV treatments, and St John’s wort can reduce protection. Not every medicine in those groups interacts in the same way.

A pharmacist or clinician can advise on another contraceptive method or additional non-hormonal protection, including how long it is needed after an interacting medicine stops. Do not stop necessary treatment yourself or assume that adding another hormonal pill solves the interaction.

Removal, warning signs and your next plan

You can request removal at any time, including for side effects or a wish to conceive. A trained clinician removes it; a deeply placed or non-palpable implant may need imaging and specialist care. Arrange replacement or another method immediately if you want continued pregnancy prevention.

Seek urgent same-day assessment if pregnancy is possible and you have lower abdominal pain or unusual vaginal bleeding, even without a positive test. Ectopic pregnancy must be considered. Severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy vaginal bleeding or breathing difficulty, needs immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself.

Get emergency help for sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, stroke-like symptoms or a severe allergic reaction. These symptoms are not expected adjustment effects. Most users will not have a serious complication, but a new concerning symptom should not be dismissed just because an implant is present.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The January 2026 US Nexplanon label and current NHS pages describe five-year use; confirm the actual product and local advice.

Bleeding changes may persist; evaluation and management should follow the person’s preferences.

Starting and switching need pregnancy assessment and clear instructions about additional protection.

Product contraindications, national eligibility guidance and individual circumstances require professional review.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record the product name, fitting date, replacement plan, bleeding changes and questions for the appointment. A record can support care; it cannot confirm implant position, exclude pregnancy or determine whether a medicine interacts.

When to seek help

Contact the service for a missing or changing implant, arm infection or neurological symptoms, or troublesome bleeding. Possible pregnancy with lower abdominal pain or unusual vaginal bleeding needs urgent same-day assessment even without a positive test. Severe or worsening pelvic or abdominal pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, heavy vaginal bleeding or breathing difficulty, needs emergency help now. Chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, stroke-like symptoms or a severe allergic reaction also need immediate emergency help. Do not drive yourself. This article does not replace individualized contraceptive advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check the exact product and local replacement date; five-year Nexplanon guidance is current in the US and NHS.
  • Bleeding can change in several directions and may stay troublesome; ask about options.
  • Do not stop your existing contraception before switching without a coordinated plan.
  • Review interacting medicines, and do not use BMI alone as a failure cutoff.
  • Only a trained professional should fit, locate or remove an implant.

Frequently asked questions

What is a contraceptive implant?

It is a small hormone-releasing rod placed beneath the upper-arm skin by a trained clinician. It mainly suppresses ovulation and thickens cervical mucus.

Does every implant need replacing after three years?

No. Current US Nexplanon labeling and NHS information describe five years. Other products or local instructions may differ; confirm your own replacement date with the service.

What are its main advantages?

It is highly effective, long acting and does not require a daily pill or interruption during sex. It is estrogen free, can be used while breastfeeding with suitable advice, and is removable when you want.

Who should discuss another option?

People with possible pregnancy, unexplained bleeding, relevant cancers, liver or vascular conditions, or component allergies need a clinical suitability review. Do not decide from a checklist alone.

Will my periods stop?

They might, but they may instead become lighter, irregular or prolonged. Your pattern cannot be predicted reliably. Ask for help if changes are unacceptable.

Can I use it if my BMI is over 30?

Obesity alone is not a reason to assume implant failure or exclude use. Review the actual product, health conditions and medicines with your clinician.

Should I stop the pill before the appointment?

Do not create a gap yourself. The switching plan may involve continuing your current method briefly and using extra protection. Get instructions for your particular situation.

Can I get pregnant immediately after removal?

Fertility can return quickly, even before a first period. Pregnancy is not guaranteed. Arrange contraception immediately after removal if pregnancy is not wanted.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
